Nonprofit award disruption, 2025–26

Source: vignettes/articles/disruption-2025.Rmd
disruption-2025.Rmd

How many active federal awards to nonprofits were disrupted after January 20, 2025? Every grant and contract held by a matched nonprofit that was scheduled to be running on 20 January 2025, followed for days and compared with the same window starting 20 January 2023.

Data through Draft · preliminary

This article applies the method in vignette("disruption") to the whole nonprofit population: every UEI in the npmatch nonprofit crosswalk (141,420 UEIs), pulled from the USAspending annual award archives for FY2008–FY2026. That database is not shipped with the package, so the article draws from pre-computed tables (data-raw/report_articles.R copies them in). Two companion articles go further: Disruption on the ledger shows what disruption looked like action by action, and Obligation trends, FY2026 shows how far new money fell below trend.

The short answer

Which signals moved

Each award is read for the signals us_disruption_flags() defines, then placed in one category, in this order: terminated (formal notice or code), terminated (quiet end-date cut to within 90 days of the action), reduced (early de-obligation, ceiling cut, or a shortened schedule), stalled (an annually funded award whose next funding is more than 120 days overdue, or stop-work language). The 2023 cohort is the counterfactual: the same rules, the same window length, two years earlier.

Share of active awards showing each signal

Active awards: (2025) and (2023 baseline). An award can show several signals; the category rows at top are exclusive.

When the terminations came

Awards receiving their first formal termination signal, by month

Formal terminations only (action code E/F/N or termination language, not rescinded). Recent months are incomplete: contract actions post up to ~90 days late.

By originating agency

Agency is the awarding agency on the award’s first action, so USAID awards transferred to State stay with USAID. Terminations are the cleanest comparison; the full category breakdown follows.

Share of active awards terminated (formal or quiet), by agency

Agencies with at least 600 active awards in 2025, sorted by the 2025 rate.

2023 baseline2025

How much money

Three measures, because a termination notice usually moves no money. Obligated at T0 is the award’s net obligation on 20 January 2025. Cash at stake is what the outlay model expected the award to pay out in FY2025 and later, given its ledger as it stood on 20 January 2025: the money that was still to arrive. De-obligated and ceiling cut are the formal reductions recorded in the window.

By organization size

Size is the organization’s IRS revenue (Business Master File), raised to its largest single year of federal obligations where the BMF figure is smaller, since federal awards are revenue: small < $1M, medium $1M–$10M, large ≥ $10M.

Largest disrupted awards by cash at stake

What this measure misses

  • Freezes with no recorded action. An award whose payments stop without a termination, de-obligation or end-date change is invisible to ledger flags. The eight EPA Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund awards in this population ($20B obligated to Climate United Fund, Coalition for Green Capital, Power Forward Communities and others) have no recorded action of any kind between 20 January 2025 and , so they are counted as not disrupted here. File C shows why: the money was paid out in full by December 2024 (see What was actually paid).
  • Subawards. The annual archives carry prime awards only. Nonprofits that receive federal money as subrecipients (through states, universities, or other nonprofits) are not measured.
  • Reporting lag. Contract actions post up to ~90 days late and assistance up to ~30, so the last months of the window undercount.
  • Re-awards. Work moved to a new award (same or different organization) reads as a termination of the old one; linking them is a matching problem not attempted here.
  • Organization matching. Organizations come from the npmatch UEI-to-EIN crosswalk. A few large recipients are matched to a sibling EIN (Washington University → its student-media EIN; MITRE → MITRE Engenuity); the federal-revenue floor on size corrects their size class, not their name.

What was actually paid

The ledger records decisions; outlays record payments. For every disrupted award, and for a stratified sample of undisrupted ones, the account-level outlays agencies report in File C were pulled from USAspending (POST /awards/funding/): The comparison uses only outlay reporters, meaning awards with a positive outlay in some quarter between October 2022 and December 2024, so an agency that does not report outlays (DoD, largely) never reads as non-payment. Control-sample results are weighted to the undisrupted non-DoD awards they represent.

Awards that stopped paying with money still owed

Paid in the year before 20 January 2025, still scheduled to run past April 2026, at least 10% of obligations unpaid on 20 January 2025, and no outlay at all from July 2025 through June 2026.

Next steps

  • Freeze detection across all undisrupted awards. The control sample shows that ledger flags miss most State and USAID stoppages; a full File C pull of the 120,618 undisrupted awards not yet sampled (about 2 days of API time at the observed rate) would count them all.
  • A 2023 payment baseline. Pulling File C for the 2023 cohort would put the no-cash and stopped-paying rates on the same footing as the ledger flags.
  • The last failures. 423 awards still failed after two retries (the API rejected about 16% of requests throughout); one more pass should recover most.

Sources

Built with usaspend (main @ 22aa2c9: pooled outlay model, dur_bin × late_start × short_family; us_disruption_flags()). Pipeline scripts 20–27 build the nonprofit database (tables disruption_active_2025, disruption_active_2023, filec_award_quarter, payment_stopped). Outlays: File C via us_fetch_outlays(), pulled 18–19 September 2026. Universe: grants, cooperative agreements and contracts; loans, direct payments, insurance and IDV vehicles excluded, and Defense Logistics Agency supply orders excluded as routine churn.
